key_concepts: Time complexity comparison (Binary vs. Linear search)

facts.claim: Binary search only works on data that is already sorted in a specific order (ascending or descending).
facts.explanation: If the list is not sorted, eliminating half of the elements based on size does not guarantee that the target value is excluded or included correctly.

facts.claim: Binary search cuts the search space in half with each comparison.
facts.explanation: Instead of checking every single item one by one, binary search checks the middle item and immediately discards half of the remaining items.

facts.claim: The time complexity of binary search is O(log n), making it significantly faster for large datasets than linear search which is O(n).
facts.explanation: As the dataset grows larger, linear search takes proportionally more time, whereas binary search increases in steps very slowly.

facts.claim: Binary search compares the target value to the middle element of the array to decide whether to search the left or right half.
facts.explanation: This comparison drives the iterative or recursive splitting process of the algorithm.

conflicting_information: Beginners often confuse whether binary search can be applied to linked lists efficiently; while possible, random access is slow in linked lists, making binary search impractical for them without modification.

gaps.question: Should the lesson cover the difference between iterative and recursive implementations of binary search?
gaps.reason: For an introductory 10-minute beginner lesson, diving into recursion might add unnecessary complexity, but mentioning it could be relevant depending on the curriculum path.
